slots.practicalActivity: If you have access to a Fabric tenant, open the Fabric Admin portal and note which tenant-level switches live there (who can create workspaces, external sharing, capacity assignment). If you don't have access, list from the lesson the three or four settings you'd check first as a new Fabric admin and why each matters for governance.
slots.deliverable: A short written note on the key tenant/capacity-level governance settings and why each matters.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch a domain structure for an organization with three business units, then for one workspace under one domain, assign the four workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) to four different hypothetical people and write one sentence justifying each assignment.
slots.deliverable: A sketched domain structure plus a four-role workspace assignment with justification for each role.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one lakehouse or warehouse you have access to (or imagine a sample Sales lakehouse). List who should be able to read it, who should be able to write to it, and who should only see it through a governed semantic model rather than querying the raw tables directly.
slots.deliverable: A written access breakdown (read / write / semantic-model-only) for one real or imagined lakehouse.

slots.practicalActivity: From a lakehouse's "..." menu, open Manage OneLake security (preview) and walk the New role wizard: scope it to Selected data on one table, then write the SQL WHERE-clause row filter you'd use to restrict that role to one slice of the table (for example, one country or region column). Note which other item a OneLake shortcut would need the same row filter applied to, since a shortcut doesn't carry its own independent security.
slots.deliverable: A sketched OneLake security role with a written row-security WHERE clause for one real or sample table, plus a shortcut governance note.

slots.practicalActivity: OneLake security lab: build a complete OneLake security role end to end -- name it, scope it to Selected data on one table, write both a row-security WHERE clause and a column-security exclusion list, add at least one member, then write one sentence on each of the three places (notebook, SQL analytics endpoint, Power BI report) that filter would actually be enforced.
slots.deliverable: A complete OneLake security role (row + column rules, named members) with enforcement points identified.

lessons.title: Row-Level and Column-Level Security in Fabric

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch an RLS role named "Eastern US" for a Sales semantic model: write a static DAX filter (Region = "East") and a dynamic version using USERPRINCIPALNAME() against a SalesRepEmail column. Then write the equivalent T-SQL CREATE SECURITY POLICY statement you'd use to enforce the same row filter directly on a Warehouse table, assuming a predicate function already exists.
slots.deliverable: Two DAX RLS filter expressions (static and dynamic) plus one equivalent T-SQL CREATE SECURITY POLICY statement for the same rule.

slots.practicalActivity: Name one sensitivity label from the previous slot that should block export to an unprotected format, and write one sentence on the information-protection policy that would enforce it. Then list three activities in Fabric's activity log you'd want an alert on (a sensitivity label downgrade, a bulk export, a permission change) and why each one matters.
slots.deliverable: One information-protection enforcement rule, plus a list of three alert-worthy activity-log events with reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: Security lab: for the RLS role sketched earlier, write out how you would validate it with Test as role and View as a specific person before trusting it in production, then add an Object-Level Security rule (via Tabular Editor's Roles grid, described conceptually) that hides one sensitive column entirely from a role that should never see it exists.
slots.deliverable: A written RLS validation plan (Test as role / View as) plus one OLS rule hiding a specific column from a named role.

slots.practicalActivity: Search the OneLake catalog (or, without access, list the search terms and filters you'd use) for an item related to the lakehouse you worked with earlier, and note which metadata -- endorsement status, description, domain, owner -- actually tells you whether to trust the item before building on it.
slots.deliverable: A short note on the OneLake catalog metadata fields that signal whether an item is trustworthy to reuse.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the criteria you'd require before endorsing an item as Certified rather than just Promoted. Then open lineage view for one of your own Fabric workspaces (workspace toolbar icon, or an item's "..." menu, View lineage). Pick any report and trace it backward: what semantic model feeds it, what feeds that model, and is there a warning icon anywhere in the chain?
slots.deliverable: Written Certified-vs-Promoted endorsement criteria, plus a traced upstream lineage chain for one real report with any warning flags noted.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lineage chain traced in the previous slot, run (or imagine running) impact analysis on the upstream-most item: list every downstream report, dataset, or dataflow -- including ones in other workspaces -- that would break if that item's schema changed, and one step you'd take before making the change.
slots.deliverable: A list of downstream items an impact-analysis run would surface for a real lineage chain, plus one pre-change mitigation step.

slots.practicalActivity: For the semantic model you applied RLS to earlier, write one governance rule that would let a business analyst build their own report on top of it (self-service) without ever seeing the raw lakehouse tables or bypassing the RLS/OLS you already defined.
slots.deliverable: One written governance rule enabling self-service reporting on a governed semantic model without bypassing its security.

slots.practicalActivity: Name one Fabric item type whose lineage and sensitivity labels would show up in Microsoft Purview once the tenant is connected, and one governance question that visibility answers for an auditor outside the Fabric team. Then, following the lesson's case study pattern, write a short governance review for one real Fabric workspace you've worked with: its domains, workspace roles, OneLake security, and endorsement state.
slots.deliverable: One named Purview-visible Fabric artifact with its audit value, plus a short governance review of one real Fabric workspace.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: complete the course's own Fabric Governance Practice Lab, then assemble everything built across this course into a one-page Fabric governance package for a single workspace -- domain placement, workspace roles, a OneLake security role (row + column), an RLS/OLS-protected semantic model, endorsement status, and the lineage/impact-analysis chain traced for its key report.
slots.deliverable: The completed Fabric Governance Practice Lab plus a one-page Fabric governance package covering domains, roles, OneLake security, model security, endorsement, and lineage for one workspace.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can configure domains, workspace roles, and OneLake row/column security in Microsoft Fabric, apply and validate row-level and object-level security on a real semantic model with DAX and T-SQL, trace lineage and run impact analysis across a multi-item Fabric workspace, and connect that governance picture to Purview -- closing out the Data Governance Engineer path's hands-on platform coverage.
